THE FORGOTTEN ORIGINS OF NEURAL NETWORKS 59 technologists in the field of financial services, the innovation is staggering and, like electricity before it, has the potential to transform how financial transactions are conducted, shaping the next generation of credit decisioning. What should the reader expect from this chapter? Unlike the previous chapter’s linear progression through logistic regression’s development, this chapter weaves together multiple historical threads to tell a more complex story, which may be particularly interesting to technologists. Our goal is neither to provide a historical timeline of AI’s developmenta nor an overview of the mathematics underpinning modern AI models. Instead, we trace how credit risk modeling evolved on a parallel track to mainstreamAI. Throughout this chapter, we will talk extensively about machines—be they hypothetical ones like Turing’s unorganised machines or practical devices like Fair and Isaac’s scorecards. We begin this chapter with the forgotten origins of neural networks in the 1940s and 1950s, tracing their roots to Alan M. Turing’s work on computability theory and revealing how his ideas about learning machines preceded the famous Perceptron. The chapter then explores the “AI spring” with the introduction of backpropagation for training multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), which form the foundation of today’s AI systems. We also provide mathematical details on simple neural networks and introduce several use cases for AI in credit risk and financial services more broadly. aFor a concise and widely used introduction, see Chapter 1 of Deep Learning by Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville [7]. Readers interested in earlier foundational work may explore Ivakhnenko’s 1960s deep architectures (often considered the first modern multilayer networks) and Schmidhuber’s historical surveys, which document the evolution of deep learning in greater detail. For a more technical introduction to neural networks, I recommend [25] and [22]. 3.1 The Forgotten Origins of Neural Networks The advances in computability theory by Alan Turing, Alonzo Church, and John von Neumann laid the groundwork for researchers to develop computational models of neural processes and cognition. The history of neural networks o�cially starts with Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts, whose 1943 paper introduced the first mathematical model of artificial neurons [13]. Building directly on Turing’s work2 on “Computable Numbers” [27], they established a basic framework: simple computational units that could be connected together to perform logical operations. Each artificial neuron would sum its inputs and fire (output 1) or remain silent (output 0) based on whether the sum exceeded a threshold—a binary decision rule that could implement logical operations like AND (∧), OR (∨), and NOT (¬). Yet John von Neumann recognized a paradox in this achievement. “After the great positive contribution of Turing-cum-Pitts-and-McCulloch is assimilated,” he observed, “the situation is rather worse than better than before. Indeed these authors have demonstrated in absolute and hopeless generality that anything and everything . . . can be done by an appropriate mechanism, 2The conceptual connections between McCulloch-Pitts neurons and Turing’s theory of computation were later articulated by John von Neumann [16], who helped bridge neuroscience, logic, and the emerging field of computer science.

60 CHAPTER 3. DEEP LEARNING: CREDIT RISK AND WAVES OF AI and specifically by a neural mechanism—and that even one, definite mechanism can be ‘universal’ ” [5]. Universal computability was profound in theory, but it o�ered no practical guidance: how should one actually configure these mechanisms to perform useful tasks? Five years after McCulloch and Pitts, in a little-known report entitled “Intelligent Machinery,” Alan Turing proposed an answer [26]. Rather than hand-wiring neural circuits for specific computations, what if the network could learn, randomly? Turing called his creation “unorganised machines,” specifically B-type unorganised machines. While McCulloch and Pitts had shown how to wire neurons together to compute specific logical functions, Turing asked a di�erent question: what if neurons were connected randomly, and the network learned through modification and training? As Copeland and Proudfoot [3] observe, Turing was probably the first to consider building computing machines from simple, neuron-like elements connected in largely random networks, then training them through experience. Turing’s paper demonstrated that such unorganised machines could be conditioned to learn— essentially inventing the concept of trainable neural networks [28]. His ideas went beyond the static logical circuits of McCulloch and Pitts to explore how networks could adapt and improve, a conceptual advance that anticipated modern deep learning by decades. 3.2 Perceptron Yet this work remained largely unknown. When Frank Rosenblatt, a psychologist working at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory, developed the Perceptron in 1958—coining the term “connectionist” and building the first hardware implementation of a learning neural network—he appears to have been unaware of Turing’s earlier exploration [21]. The parallel is striking: just as Turing had written his doctoral thesis on Gaussian errors without knowing the topic had been addressed by Jarl Waldemar Lindeberg a decade earlier, Rosenblatt independently rediscovered ideas that Turing had sketched ten years prior [3]. The Perceptron can be understood as a neural network consisting of a single artificial neuron with a threshold activation function and a single layer of weights (analogous to coe�cients in a regression model). It processes Boolean-encoded input patterns (recall the one-hot encoding we covered in Chapter 2) and adjusts its weights through a learning rule. Rosenblatt’s learning algorithm drew inspiration from Donald Hebb’s 1949 work on synaptic plasticity [8], which proposed that connections between neurons strengthen when they fire together: the famous neuroscience principle “cells that fire together, wire together.” This Hebbian learning rule provided a biological foundation for how artificial networks might adapt through experience. A reader may notice a striking resemblance between the Perceptron and logistic regression. Both compute a weighted sum of inputs and make predictions based on whether this sum exceeds a threshold. The key di�erence is in the activation function: the Perceptron uses a step function (outputting 0 or 1), while logistic regression uses the smooth sigmoid function (outputting probabilities between 0 and 1). Due to this property, logistic regression can be interpreted as a neural network without any hidden layers [1]. The Perceptron computes: ŷ = { 1 if ∑n i=1 wixi + b > 0 0 otherwise (3.1)

Rosenblatt’s learning algorithmupdatedweights iteratively based on errors, though it predated modern gradient descent and backpropagation. The Perceptron’s fundamental limitation, its inability to learn the exclusive OR (XOR, ⊕) problem, was famously demonstrated by Minsky and Papert in 1969 [14]. The XOR (⊕) problem requires classifying cases where exactly one of two conditions holds, but not both or neither: High Debt Low Income Risky? No No No No Yes Yes Yes No Yes Yes Yes No A single Perceptron cannot solve this problem, as it can only create linear decision boundaries. This limitation contributed to the first AI winter that lasted until the mid-1980s.

DEEP LEARNING: CREDIT RISK AND WAVES OF AI 3.3 The First AI Winter and Credit Risk’s Quiet Revolution The Perceptron’s limitations contributed to what became known as the first AI winter, a period of reduced funding and interest that lasted until the mid-1980s. Yet while academic AI research struggled, something remarkable happened in the practical world of finance: credit scoring became one of machine learning’s earliest commercial successes. In 1956, the same summer that John McCarthy coined the term “artificial intelligence” at the Dartmouth workshop where researchers gathered to make machines “use language, form abstractions, and solve problems reserved for humans,” two parallel revolutions were emerging. While AI pioneers theorized general artificial intelligence, Bill Fair and Earl Isaac, each investing $400, established Fair Isaac Corporation to develop and market their credit scoring concept [20]. Their timing was fortuitous: lending o�ces and credit bureaus were already collecting the structured data that would power a di�erent kind of intelligent machine. In 1957, Fair Isaac began work focused on what it called “the credit granting problem”—the specific challenge of account origination and risk selection in consumer finance. Just as neural network researchers would later grapple with the “credit assignment problem” (determining how much each component of a network contributed to the final output), Fair Isaac was solving its own credit assignment problem—determining how much credit to assign to each applicant based on their contribution to predicted risk. By 1958, the world’s first commercial credit scoring systems for predicting consumer default had been developed and installed. Ranking Odds: The Scorecard Machinery Scorecards work by placing individual cases in relationship to a record of proven outcomes [18]. The device compares information about a prospective borrower to empirical patterns found at the population level, captured from accumulated historical data. By standardizing information requirements (set questions with defined answer choices), processing these data through a problem-specific algorithm, and expressing output on a numerical scale, this technology provides managers with probabilistic information for making operating decisions. The name itself was strategic. Fair Isaac called their tool used to calculate empirical likelihood of default a “scorecard,” presumably to make it familiar by associating it with the point systems in sports. The name highlighted the technology’s two most obvious features: the numerical score output and the physical card format (which has now gone obsolete but we can still encounter it now in the digital form). Table 3.1 shows an actual scorecard from 1977 [23], which FICO made publicly available. Each characteristic (years on job, bank accounts, credit bureau rating) has associated point values based on how borrowers with those attributes had historically performed.

64 CHAPTER 3. DEEP LEARNING: CREDIT RISK AND WAVES OF AI Engineering for Simplicity Yet the scorecard was not an innovation that the credit industry developed on its own. Its development required bringing together statistical theory, practical business needs, and the emerging data infrastructure of credit bureaus. Fair Isaac’s approach succeeded precisely because it didn’t require general intelligence. The problem was well-defined: predict default using historical patterns to avoid negative outcomes in future decisions. Although Fair Isaac inherited its philosophical outlook from cybernetic theories of control and communication [20], their solution was pragmatic rather than theoretical. Their innovation was a decision science device called a “scorecard”—designed as “an accurate odds quoter” of an applicant’s future behavior [18]. Early scorecards served as aids for determining whether credit should be granted to prospective applicants based on their responses to a series of set questions. The system was carefully engineered for simplicity: credit applicants answered questions (in person or on application forms) that could be classified in tables printed on cards, with associated point values added up to produce a “credit score.” This score represented the empirically assessed odds that a person with a particular combination of characteristics, compared against known outcomes of a lender’s population of clients, would default on a loan. The design reflected practical constraints. The score needed to be simple because those calculating or interpreting it were unlikely to have statistical training (recall from Chapter 1 how deciban rounding made the job of Turing’s associates simpler). Fair Isaac collected data from lenders and bureaus, working with paper-based records. Data scientists—then called “analysts”— had to figure out, on the ground, how to constitute samples that could build statistical models adequately discriminating between “good” and “bad” risk. According to statistical theory, and confirmed by Fair Isaac’s empirical tests, a scoring model’s predictive utility was intimately bound to the parameters of the data set from which it was modeled [19]. Early scorecards mechanically replicated choices previously made by lenders, but refined this replication by sorting populations into statistically di�erentiated groups, each assigned di�erent odds of repayment. The Bridge That Never Was: Neural Networks and Credit Scoring By the 1960s, Fair Isaac’s credit scoring system was already transforming consumer lending proving that better credit decisions did not require complex methods as opposed to good data and sound statistical principles. Throughout the AI winters and summers that followed, credit risk modeling evolved steadily but conservatively, prioritizing interpretability, reproducibility, and regulatory defensibility. This conservative evolution created a profound divergence. While AI researchers pursued ever more sophisticated architectures—from backpropagation in the 1980s to deep learning in the 2010s—credit scoring remained anchored to simpler methods. The reasons were practical: lenders needed to explain their decisions to regulators, justify adverse actions to applicants, and maintain stable models that would not fluctuate wildly with each model recalibration. Neural networks, with their opaque layers and sensitivity to training data, o�ered power but not the transparency credit decisions demanded. 3.4 Multilayer Networks and Backpropagation The limitation of single-layer perceptrons exposed byMinsky and Papert [14] had a straightforward solution, though it would take nearly two decades to fully realize: add more layers (and di�erent

3.4. MULTILAYER NETWORKS AND BACKPROPAGATION 65 activations as will be discovered later). A network with multiple layers of neurons—what we now call amultilayer perceptron (MLP), also known as feedforward deep networks—can learn non-linear decision boundaries, including XOR and far more complex patterns (Figure 3.3). Figure 3.3: A deep neural network architecture with multiple hidden layers. Unlike the single- layer Perceptron, this network can learn complex non-linear patterns by composing multiple layers of weighted connections. Each layer transforms its inputs, allowing the network to build increasingly abstract representations from input to output. The theoretical foundation for this had existed since the 1960s, but a practical obstacle remained: how to e�ciently train these deeper networks? Backpropagation: A Game-Changer Before 1986, training multi-layer neural networks was largely intractable. The breakthrough came with backpropagation, the algorithm that would awaken neural networks from their first winter. At its core, backpropagation solves a practical problem: in a multi-layer network, how do we know which weights to adjust and by how much? The answer lies in tracing errors backward through the network, layer by layer. Though the core idea had been independently discovered multiple times—by Paul Werbos in his 1974 PhD thesis [29], and later by David Parker [17] and Yann Le Cun [12]—it was the 1986 paper “Learning Representations by Back-Propagating Errors” by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams [9] that brought the algorithm to widespread attention. The impact of this work proved transformative: Geo�rey Hinton, one of the paper’s authors, received the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics “for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks” [24]. The backpropagation algorithm’s popularity stems from being conceptually simple, computa- tionally e�cient, and because it often works [15].

In the forward pass (Step 1), we compute predictions: inputs x1 and x2 flow through the hidden layer (using weightsw(1)) to produce hidden activations, which then flow to the output ŷ (using weightsw(2)). We compare ŷ to the true value and compute a loss L. The backward pass (Step 2, backpropagation) works in reverse. Starting from the loss, we ask: how much did each weight contribute to the error? For the output layer weights w(2), this is straightforward—we can see their direct impact on the prediction. But for the hidden layer weights w(1), the connection is indirect: they a�ect the hidden activations, which in turn a�ect the output, which a�ects the loss. Backpropagation uses the chain rule from calculus to decompose this. The complete forward and backward passes can be expressed compactly. Note that each layer includes a bias term b (an additive constant) that allows the activation function σ (representing any di�erentiable nonlinearity, such as sigmoid or tanh) to shift left or right, giving the network more flexibility to fit the data: Forward pass: h = σ(w(1) · x+ b(1)) (hidden layer) (3.2) ŷ = σ(w(2) · h+ b(2)) (output layer) (3.3) Backward pass (gradients): ∂L ∂w(2) = ∂L ∂ŷ × ∂ŷ ∂w(2) (output layer weights) (3.4) ∂L ∂w(1) = ∂L ∂ŷ × ∂ŷ ∂h × ∂h ∂w(1) (hidden layer weights) (3.5) Put di�erently, the impact of a hidden layer weight equals (how loss changes with the output) × (how output changes with hidden activations) × (how hidden activations change with that weight). By computing these gradients layer by layer in reverse, backpropagation e�ciently determines how to adjust every weight in the network.

Figure 3.5: Neural network solving the XOR problem. Before training (left), the data shows an XOR pattern with red and blue classes in diagonally opposite regions. After training (right), the network learns a non-linear decision boundary (probability heatmap) that correctly classifies both classes - something impossible for single-layer models. This case demonstrates the universal approximation theorem in action. The universal approxi- mation theorem, proven independently by Cybenko [4] and Hornik [10], provides a powerful theoretical guarantee: a neural network with just a single hidden layer, the one we have in our model, can approximate any continuous function to arbitrary accuracy, given enough neurons and the right weights. However, the theorem only guarantees that such weights exist. It says nothing about: • Whether we can actually find those weights through training • How many neurons we’d need in practice (often impractically many) • Whether the network will generalize well to new data This is why deeper networks, those with many layers, often work better in practice. While one hidden layer is theoretically su�cient, multiple layers can learn the same functions with fewer total neurons, discovering hierarchical patterns (like edges → features → objects) that mirror how complex problems are naturally structured. Digital banking and real-time payments now generate continuous streams of transaction information rather than isolated, static snapshots. Mobile applications expose spending rhythms, payment timing, and behavioral signals that traditional credit reports never captured. With the advent of

DEEP LEARNING: CREDIT RISK AND WAVES OF AI open banking, lenders can access months of granular transaction history—often with far richer temporal structure than anything previously available. This shift from static attributes to dynamic behavioral trajectories creates an environment where deep learning is not merely an alternative to traditional scoring models, but a natural extension. Classic scorecards distill a borrower into fixed snapshots: current debt-to-income ratio, number of recent delinquencies, total credit utilization. Transaction sequences, by contrast, reveal how income fluctuates and how spending behavior adapts to the economy. Deep learning models, designed to exploit structure in sequences, can capture these temporal dynamics and cross-pattern interactions in ways that logistic regression or gradient boosting cannot. Where tabular credit features favor tree-based methods, transaction sequences naturally align with neural networks capable of modeling order, recurrence, and long-range dependencies. This perspective forms the foundation of cash flow underwriting: assessing creditworthiness through real-time behavioral analysis rather than static historical aggregates. Cash-Flow Underwriting Most credit risk models rely on a point-in-time snapshot of customer information. Although these snapshots can incorporate simple trend indicators, they rarely capture the full temporal structure of a borrower’s financial behavior. Scorecards, in particular, treat each variable as an independent, static attribute, leaving rich sequential patterns unmodeled. Deep learning o�ers a fundamentally di�erent approach. Many of its most influential architectures were developed precisely to handle sequences. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and their variants, such as Long Short-TermMemory networks (LSTMs), were designed to process ordered data by retaining information from previous time steps. Transformers, now the dominant architecture in sequence modeling, extend this idea using self-attention, which allows the model to weigh and relate all elements in a sequence simultaneously. This mechanism provides a flexible form of “memory” far better suited to capturing long-range dependencies than earlier methods. The combination of rich transactional data and modern computational power makes it possi- ble to apply these architectures directly to underwriting. What was once impractical—analyzing hundreds or thousands of transactions per customer—is now routine. Instead of relying solely on static attributes, we can model: • trends in income and expenditures, • fluctuations in account balances, • variance and stability of income, • clusters of spending behavior (e.g., saving, discretionary spending, stress spending), • early signals of financial deterioration or resilience. By learning from how a customer manages cash flow over time—not just from what their attributes are at a single moment—deep learning opens the door to underwriting approaches that are more dynamic, responsive, and behaviorally grounded. Training neural networks on transactional data requires careful attention to both data preprocessing and architectural choices. Key ingredients include:

3.5. CREDIT RISK IN THE AGE OF AI 73 • Feature engineering: Extract amounts, balances, and temporal changes from raw transac- tions • Balanced sampling: Use equal representation of defaults and non-defaults cases (50/50 split) during training phase • Standardization: Scale features to zero mean and unit variance • Batch normalization: Stabilize training by batch normalization • Sequential processing: Structure data as time-ordered sequences at the account level to be processed in batches The ability to collect detailed transactional histories, coupled with scalable compute, makes this shift possible. Rather than evaluating a single balance snapshot, we can analyze entire trajectories of income, expenditures, transfers, and savings patterns. From these sequences, neural networks can learn the underlying financial signatures directly: how much a customer typically spends, on what categories, how consistently they save, how volatile their cash flows are, and how they respond to periods of financial stress. In essence, transactional data allow us to reconstruct a customer’s financial life in motion, since deep learning can automatically discover the features that best predict default risk. To illustrate these ideas, consider a transformer-based model trained on real transactional data from a large lender. The model processes sequences of up to 50 transactions per customer. Instead of relying on hand-crafted features, the transformer constructs its own internal representations through multiple layers of self-attention and feed-forward layers. 74 CHAPTER 3. DEEP LEARNING: CREDIT RISK AND WAVES OF AI This highlights a key advantage of deep learning for credit risk: the ability to model the shape of financial behavior. Where a scorecard might use a single “average monthly balance” variable, a transformer considers the entire trajectory of those balances—how they rise and fall, when they spike or collapse, and how these movements relate to the timing and magnitude of individual transactions. Such temporal richness was historically inaccessible to traditional approaches but is now central to modern, behaviorally informed underwriting. Underwriting Agents A second frontier in the application of AI to credit risk is the automation of routine underwriting tasks. Much of underwriting consists not of subjective judgment but of a sequence of highly structured checks: retrieving bureau and bank data, validating documentation, confirming model outputs, and ensuring that a decision complies with internal policy. These steps follow clear procedural logic, making them well suited for automation through agentic AI systems. Recent advances in large language models (LLM) make it possible to build multi-agent underwriting workflows, where each AI agent specializes in a specific part of the process. One agent may extract key financial attributes from an application or a bank statement; another may retrieve credit scores; a third may verify that a recommended action is consistent with the lending policy. These agents can communicate with one another through a form of structured message passing and present their findings to a human underwriter who owns decision-making. This human-in-the-loop approach o�ers several advantages. It accelerates decision making by o�oading repetitive checks, increases consistency by enforcing standardized procedures, and produces an auditable trail of intermediate reasoning steps. Importantly, these systems do not replace existing risk methodologies. Instead, they orchestrate them by retrieving the necessary data, and ensuring that all conditions for a compliant decision are met. Viewed in this way, an “AI underwriter” is not a single monolithic model but a coordinated ensemble of specialized agents, each performing a narrow task. The analogy to human under- writing is direct: junior analysts collect documents and run checks, while senior underwriters synthesize the results and make the final decision. AI agents operate similarly, with the crucial di�erence that their “training” occurs through prompt-based instruction fine-tuning. However, deploying such systems within financial services requires particular care. Most underwriting workflows cannot rely on externally hosted, general-purpose language models: doing so introduces data-privacy risks, creates dependencies on third-party infrastructure, limits reproducibility, andmakes it di�cult to demonstrate determinism to regulators. For these reasons, the safest and most practical approach is to deploy local or institution-hosted open-weights LLMs, either fine-tuned or prompt-adapted to the lender’s own credit policies, documentation standards, and operational constraints. Within this setup, two capabilities are especially important. First, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds an agent’s reasoning in approved internal documents—policies, procedures, model governance reports, and historical cases—by retrieving relevant excerpts at query time. This ensures that the model bases its reasoning on verifiable institutional knowledge and behaves deterministically: given the same inputs, it will always produce the same outputs.

Second, tool-calling allows the AI underwriter to interact with internal systems such as credit bureau interfaces, income-verification tools, scoring engines, or document repositories through controlled and auditable functions that are maintained by the lender. This provides a safe way for an LLM to trigger external actions while keeping every step transparent and reproducible. Together, local open-weights LLMs, RAG, and tool-calling form a controllable and auditable agentic framework for underwriting. When aligned with a lender’s internal policies and processes, these systems can automate substantial portions of the workflow while maintaining consistency, determinism, and full regulatory traceability. Towards Credit Risk AI This chapter has traced a remarkable arc: fromTuring’s 1948 vision of “unorganisedmachines” that could learn through experience, through the AI winters and the rediscovery of backpropagation, to today’s transformer architectures and agentic AI systems. What began as a theoretical question— canmachines learn?—has evolved into practical systems that can now assist in credit underwriting, transaction monitoring, and risk assessment. The parallel evolution of credit scoring and neural networks is particularly noteworthy. While Fair and Isaac were building their first scorecards in the 1950s using hand-crafted features and

76 References linear algorithms, researchers were exploring how networks of artificial neurons might learn on their own. Both approaches sought to automate human judgment, but through fundamentally di�erent philosophies: one through careful feature engineering and interpretable odds-based risk measurements, the other through adaptive learning in high-dimensional spaces. Today, these traditions converge. Modern credit risk systems combine the interpretability and regulatory acceptance of traditional scorecards with the pattern-recognition capabilities of deep learning. MLPs extract nonlinear relationships from transaction sequences, transformers attend to temporal patterns in payment histories, and agentic systems orchestrate these models within compliant underwriting workflows. Yet the challenge remains: how can lenders, both large and small, build on these new foundations without undermining the legacy systems that regulators understand and trust? The thirdwave ofAI o�ers unprecedented capabilities, but also unprecedented responsibilities. Turing’s unorganised machines have finally arrived, but their successful deployment in credit risk will depend not just on their technical sophistication but on our wisdom in applying them. The question is no longer whether neural networks can learn credit risk patterns—they demonstrably can—but whether they can do so in ways that satisfy regulatory requirements for transparency, fairness, and stability. As we deploy these systems in financial services, we must ensure they enhance rather than obscure the decision-making process, that they reduce rather than amplify bias, and that they remain robust under the distributional shifts that inevitably occur in credit markets.
